MATERNAL SEPSIS DURING & FOLLOWING PREGNANCY

WHO definition of Sepsis:

Organ dysfunction resulting from infection during pregnancy, child Birth, Post abortion or post-partum period.

Septic shock:

Persistent hypotension, requiring vasopressor to maintain an adequate B.P (MAP 65mmhg or more). Alongside an increase in serum lactate >2mmol despite adequate volume replacement.

Risk Factors:

Maternal:

Obesity

Impaired glucose tolerance.

Anemia.

DM

Age > 35.

GAS in contact.

GBS carriage.

Pelvic infection.

Obstetric Risk Factors:

SROM.

Amniocentesis.

Vaginal delivery.

C/Section.

Cervical cerclage.

Important one liner:

Most common infection = pneumonia 44%.

2nd most common = UTI 20%.

Most common agent = E. coli.

2nd most common = GBS – lesser mortality than GAS.

GAS commonly present within 12 hours of abortion/ Birth with persistent Bleeding and Pain + feeling unwell.

GAS => increased mortality.

0.03 – 0.06% have perineal colonization with GAS & are Asymptomatic, vaginal discharge is often watery, leukocytes are destroyed by GAS leucocidins and not offensive.

Chorioamnionitis = mixed infection.

UTI, cerclage, PPROM = coliform bacteria.

Rule out Allergies to A/B:

Careful history Nausea/ Vomiting => intolerance not allergy.

Mild rash with penicillin => 1 – 3% are allergic to cephalosporins/ Cross reaction.

Anaphylaxis with penicillin => Avoid

- Cephalosporin.

- carbapenem.

Discuss: infection specialist.

Alterative: Erythromycin, clindamycin, vancomycin.

Management:

MDT:

Senior obstetrician

Senior anesthetist within 1 hour

Senior Midwife

 

Expert MDT:

urgently if sepsis not responding to initial management.

Critical care Team:

Urgent referral in severe or rapidly deteriorating cases of sepsis.

Indications for Transfer to ICU:

CVS:

Hypotension < 90 mmHg systolic.

Lactate > 4 mmol/lit persistent despite fluids resuscitation.

Suggesting need for vasopressor/ inotropic support.

Respiratory:

Pulmonary edema.

Need for mechanical ventilation.

Need for airway protection.

Renal:

Renal replacement Therapy.

Neurological:

Conscious level.

Miscellaneous:

MOD

Uncorrected acidosis.

Hypothermia.

Surviving sepsis campaign Hour – 1 Bundle of care:

Measure lactate. (Re measure if > 2mmol/ lit within 1 hour).

Obtain blood cultures.

Broad spectrum antibiotics.

I/V fluids 30ml/kg crystalloids if lactate > 4.

Apply vasopressors if hypotension after fluid resuscitation to maintain B.P MAP > 65mnHg.

Antibiotics:

I/V Antibiotics within 1 hour in women @ high risk of sepsis or septic shock.

Use of sepsis bundle improve compliance with urgent management.

Early fluid resuscitation of crystalloids with immediate bolus of 500ml in women with hypotension and lactate > 4mmol, urine output be strictly monitored with urometer – 1 hourly.

Choice of A/B depends upon local epidemiology.

Where sensitivity not known = piperacillin/ tazobactam or Meropenem (for G – negative) plus clindamycin (for G – positive + Anaerobes) provide very broad cover.

Vancomycin is advisable in case of MRSA.

Switch to specific antibiotics in case availability of culture reports.

Add I/V Acyclovir 500mg TDS, as part of 2nd line A/B in case of maternal deterioration with 1st line cover.

Pyrexia in labor > 380C or high => GBS prophylaxis.

Consider VTE propylene in sepsis.

Necrotizing Fasciitis:

Post birth wound can lead to serious abdominal or perineal N.F.

Infection causing necrosis of superficial and deep and sub cutaneous tissues.

1.8/1000 C/section can lead to N.F.

Rapid for by GAS.

Spread is hematogenous or direct.

Visible signs are in later stages.

Require increasing analgesic.

increasing and out of proportion pain due to edema and thrombosis of arterial supply to nerves leading to increasing demand of analgesia.

Obvious signs are later – bruises, Blisters.

Urgent involvement of plastic surgeon, intensivist, and infection specialist.

Treatment:

Piperacillin – tazobactam

OR + clindamycin + Meropenem vanco in case of

MRSA.

Clindamycin => switch off exotoxin.

MRSA => vancomycin should be added.

Streptococcal Toxic Shock Syndrome < 50% pts have classical sunburn rash.

Staph TSS => 100% sun burn rash.

 

Resistance to these A/B or allergies => consult infection specialist.

Table 38. Important points regarding Antibiotics:

Spectrum

Points

Co – amoxiclav

No activity against MRSA or Pseudomonas Active against most streptococci, staphylococci (MSSA) anaerobes and many Gram negatives

Concern about an increase in the risk of necrotizing enterocolitis in babies exposed to co-amoxiclav in utero

Metronidazole

Only covers anaerobes

Unnecessary if using clindamycin and piperacillin-tazobactam as each covers anaerobes well

Used with e.g. cefotaxime as intrapartum prophylaxis for suspected chorioamnionitis if non-severe penicillin allergy

Clindamycin

covers most GAS (>89%) ; GBS (67%) so should no longer be used for GBS prophylaxis , Covers most staphylococci, including

many MRSA. and anaerobes Switches off exotoxin production

Not renally excreted or nephrotoxic

Associated with increased risk of Clostridium difficile superinfection

Piperacillin – tazobactam.

Spectrum same as co-amoxiclav, but also many Gram positive and Gram-negative organisms, including pseudomonas

No activity against MRSA

Renal sparing (in contrast to aminoglycosides)

Poor activity against ESBL, producing coliforms

Avoid in beta-lactam allergy Very poor CSF penetration

Cephalosporins e.g. ceftriaxone.

No activity against ESBL producing coliforms, pseudomonas or MRSA

Cover beta-haemolytic streptococci including GAS and GBS (but not enterococci)

Should not be used if severe beta-lactam allergy Increased risk of C. difficle

Carbapenems

Very broad empirical cover, most Gram-negatives (including most ESBL-producers, anaerobes) Covers most Gram positives except MRSA CPE are resistant.

Not for severe beta-lactam allergy With moderate beta-lactam allergy <1% cross reaction

Excellent penetration including CSF

Gentamicin

Mainly Gram negative cover (including most pseudomonas)

No streptococcal, or anerobic cover

Inactivated in pus/anaerobic conditions Nephrotoxic and ototoxic, so usually limited where possible to a stat dose for sepsis. (For endocarditis a lower dose is given twice daily. and then serum levels must be monitored)

Vancomycin

Covers MRSA. Recommended option in severe penicillin allergy for GBS prophylaxis.

No cover for Gram negatives.

Not absorbed orally, so always given intravenously unless treating C.difficile infection.

Serum levels need to be monitored due to the potential for renal and ototoxicity.

Too rapid infusion can cause "red man syndrome" due to histamine release.

Role of immunoglobulins:

I/V immunoglobulins should be considering as part of treatment for G positive and Toxic Shock Syndrome when other measure are failing.

Not effective for G negative or sepsis in general.

Limited use in sickest women

Use in critical care setting.

Use where blood warning device available.

Clindamycin + IVIG are reported synergistic and beneficial

C/I:

Congenital immunoglobulins A deficiency.

Dose:

2g/kg.

Fetal monitoring:

Expedite birth in critically ill women if it is beneficial.

Decision by senior obstetrician after discussion with women and/ or family.

Preterm birth:

Mgso4 and steroids should be considered.

CEFM.

Risk of neonatal encephalopathy and CP is ed in case of I/U infection.

Neonatal Care:

Babies of women treated for sepsis during labor or within 24 hours before or after birth should be assessed for neonatal infection.

If either women or baby is infected with GAS disease in post – partum period, both should be treated with Antibiotics.

Infection control strategies:

All women after birth should be informed about signs and symptoms of genital tract infection, (written + verbal) + guidance regarding hygiene, hand washing & seeking help when feel unwell.

All women identified with GAS infection during pregnancy should be aggressively treated.

All close contact with GAS infected women should seek medical advice & if symptoms develops should be treated with A/B.

All healthcare professionals who are exposed to respiratory secretions of GAS infected women should be considered for A/B.

Women with GAS infected should be cared by barrier nursing including clothing, masks, limited mobility.
